content: Effective vaccines for buffalo are available. However, further research is required to clarify the role of various animal species, such as buffalo, dogs, cats, and rats, in serving as reservoirs for disease transmission. This is particularly relevant in the Philippines, where the specific role of carabao (water buffalo) in the transmission of Schistosoma japonicum remains to be determined. Operational research is necessary to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of integrated control strategies to establish optimal approaches at scale in different geographical settings. This includes assessing the value of transmission-blocking vaccines for use in buffalo or other mammalian hosts. Research is needed to address issues of coverage and compliance related to access to mass treatment in the Philippines, particularly in Samar province, in the context of animal reservoir diversity. This will help identify which zoonotic sources significantly impact the incidence of human infections. Studies are required to investigate the effects of schistosomiasis on malnutrition and cognitive development, both in cases of single infections and polyparasitism. Improved diagnostic methods are essential in areas with low schistosomiasis prevalence and as surveillance tools to determine whether effective control has been achieved. The development of appropriate and gender-sensitive tools and methods is needed to assess the health and socioeconomic impacts of control programs on individuals and households. For foodborne trematodiases, priority research areas include estimating the global burden of these diseases, advancing the discovery and development of new diagnostic tools, vaccines, and trematocidal drugs, and determining the impact of improved access to clean water, sanitation, sewage treatment, and food safety measures. Chemotherapy-based morbidity control should remain the backbone of control programs in highly endemic areas. However, integrated control approaches and intersectoral collaboration between public health and veterinary medicine require greater attention, including considerations of feasibility, efficacy, and cost-effectiveness. Operational research on integrated control strategies, such as mass treatment, education, behavior change communication, and community-led health, sanitation, and aquaculture management, is needed in endemic communities. This should include intersectoral collaboration between public health and veterinary medicine, as well as public and private sectors, with a focus on food safety issues. Gender-specific analyses are required to understand differences in access to and compliance with foodborne trematodiases treatment. Additionally, the development of gender-sensitive tools and methods is necessary to assess the socioeconomic impact of these diseases on individuals, households, communities, and societies. National surveillance systems for foodborne trematodiases should be evaluated for their effectiveness in tracking infections. The integration of these surveillance systems with those for other zoonotic diseases should be assessed to determine their impact on health education programs for communities and schools, as well as their influence on knowledge and practices in endemic areas. For toxoplasmosis, research priorities include the development of animal vaccines, new economic and safe diagnostic techniques for acute infections during pregnancy, and cost-effective diagnostic and management protocols for central nervous system toxoplasmosis in high-risk HIV-positive patients. Additionally, culturally acceptable health education programs to improve food hygiene, particularly for pregnant women, are needed. Quantifying the impact of improved water quality and sanitation on toxoplasmosis infection rates, as well as the proportion of chronic abortions globally attributable to toxoplasmosis, is essential. For cryptosporidiosis, research priorities include documenting the burden of the disease in young children in developing countries, determining the extent of livestock as a source of Cryptosporidium infections in humans, and enhancing surveillance of infection prevalence in humans and livestock. The shortand long-term health and economic consequences for both populations should also be assessed. The impact of community-level water and sanitation improvements on human infection prevalence in urban and rural settings should be evaluated. Agricultural practices that reduce livestock exposure to infection should be identified to interrupt transmission to humans. The development of a livestock vaccine to block animal infection and reduce the excretion of infectious cysts into the environment is also a priority. For rabies, mass dog vaccination campaigns combined with prompt and appropriate post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) for individuals exposed to the rabies virus can significantly reduce human rabies incidence. However, challenges remain in developing sustainable strategies to resource this approach, including cooperation between health and veterinary sectors. Surveillance remains a major constraint in many parts of Africa and Asia, with limited laboratory diagnostic capacity and insufficient submission of diagnostic samples from clinical cases. Misdiagnosis of childhood rabies deaths as cerebral malaria in malaria-endemic areas further complicates the issue. Research priorities for rabies include the widespread use of existing techniques for field collection and storage of samples, evaluation of the cost-effectiveness of different WHO-recommended preand post-exposure regimens, and the implementation of new biological regimens for humans, such as monoclonal antibodies as a cost-effective replacement for rabies immunoglobulin. The development of innovative strategies for funding integrated and sustainable dog vaccination programs, including education and social mobilization campaigns, is essential. Combined approaches to dog rabies vaccination and immuno-contraception, as well as the economics of oral vaccination strategies for dogs, should also be investigated. For bacterial zoonoses, inexpensive, robust, and reliable diagnostic tests are needed for use in field and hospital settings. Locally appropriate cut-off points for existing tests, such as the single comparative intradermal test for bovine tuberculosis and serological tests for brucellosis, are important for acquiring valid data to inform disease burden studies. Cross-sectoral assessments of disease burden are necessary to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of interventions realistically. A common measure of zoonotic disease burden that incorporates human health indices, public health costs, livestock sector losses, and private sector costs should be developed. Ethnographic and participatory research approaches are needed to design relevant and understandable criteria for measuring impacts, considering the value of livestock for human well-being and development. For zoonotic tuberculosis in Africa, research priorities include understanding the human disease burden, identifying animal-related risk factors for human infection, and conducting clinical research on optimal drug treatment regimens for confirmed Mycobacterium bovis and non-tuberculous mycobacterial infections. For brucellosis and anthrax, livestock vaccines are available, but there is a need to ensure immunogenicity, improve vaccine safety, and design targeted vaccination strategies to optimize cost-effectiveness. Research priorities for brucellosis include assessing the immunogenic properties of current vaccines, improving their safety and immunogenicity, and designing diagnostic strategies to differentiate vaccinated animals from naturally infected ones. For enteric infections, better methods for surveillance of human enteric infections are needed, including syndromic classification and etiology in representative community settings. Clarifying reservoirs and transmission pathways for animal and human enteric infections is essential. After identifying critical points in transmission, interventions should be developed to target the most effective routes and significantly reduce their efficiency. Infrastructure and capacity to identify zoonotic enteric pathogens in relevant animal populations should be developed. The economic burden resulting from infections in livestock, including illness, market losses, and direct and indirect costs of foodborne illnesses, should be determined. Simple, cost-effective farming methods to prevent zoonotic infection transmission to animals, crops, water supplies, and humans should be tested. Communication between veterinary and human health professionals should be improved through integrated training modules and mechanisms for information exchange. Joint veterinary and human health outbreak investigation teams with access to quality laboratory diagnostic capacity should be created. Grassroots public health educational services should be enhanced to improve animal and human health outcomes. Ongoing surveillance for drug resistance should be implemented.
